event: No flight event: during the VTOL AP watchdog investigation a debug build of the VTOL autopilot firmware trapped on a null (uninitialized) semaphore.
component: VTOL AP firmware, aeroMutex semaphore in FwAero.c
failure_mode: aeroMutex was never initialized; the release-build take/give macros silently skip a null semaphore, so data shared between tasks (air data feeding navigation and an IMU correction) was unprotected
contributing: debug build configured to ignore the null semaphore exceptions
regression test matrix had no debug-build test point

evidence.quote: During testing with the debug build, it was found that one semaphore was not initialized properly, aeroMutex in FwAero.c.
It has been discovered that 32-bit writes are atomic on the processor. Therefore the impact of this bug in the current build is limited to non-existent.
Change xSemaphoreTake/GiveSafe Macros so Take/Give of NULL Semaphores can be traced.
This issue was addressed in v6.3.4. Regression test procedures were updated to account for the process gap.

team_root_cause: Non-initialized semaphore used and ignored in code. Test procedure didn’t include a test point to test with a debug build that could catch the error.
reasoning: Running a debug build with exceptions enabled trapped on the null aeroMutex in FwAero.c, which names the exact defect. The team fixed the initialization and added a debug-build test point to regression testing. The real-world impact was later judged near zero because 32-bit writes are atomic on the processor.
notes: Not a flight incident; it is a firmware and test process defect found during the WDT investigation, and the team said it was unlikely to be the cause of the WDT events. Severity was lowered in January 2024.

component: GCS Launch Wizard GPS Fix Check dialog
failure_mode: no fault: the dialog shows "Waiting for GPS Fix" and disables Next as designed, but gives no exit instruction (cancel, move or try later), so the tester expected a timeout or explicit GPS warning
contributing: Troubleshooting Quicksheet is a Block 25 PDF the operator may not know about
acceptance criteria (SRD-309) assumed a more explicit GPS indication

evidence.quote: the LW does not specifically indicate the GPS issue and instead GCS calibration window does not go past its window
In the event of no GPS fix on the vehicle, the user is presented with Status of “Waiting for GPS Fix” in the lower left hand portion of the dialog.
I think the issue might be better phrased: The pilot is trapped at this step if GPS doesn’t get a fix.
If no GPS after this step, suspect aircraft GPS failure as cause; if multiple GPS units

User expected more explicit instructions or may not have access to troubleshooting sheet.
(Original text: Misalignment between aircraft specs and acceptance criteria; likely based on expectation that the system should time-out in this stage, which we do not want to include to allow user to try adressing the issue.)

The GCS lead showed the dialog already reports Waiting for GPS Fix and disables Next. The only gap is wording and an exit instruction, which is a requirement and expectation mismatch rather than a fault.

event: VXE-487 fuselage flying with the VXE-488 center wing lost all four lift motors at about 90 to 110 ft during VTOL landing and fell to the ground, heavily damaged.
component: AS150 power contact (center wing HLB connection, 488 wing)
failure_mode: high contact resistance with visible damage (305 uOhm, 253 uOhm after cleaning, field limit 235) caused intermittent contact and arcing; HLB voltage at the lift system dropped to 7.5 V and the lift motors stopped
contributing: possible incomplete connector mate
old firmware (FWAP 6.05j, XCOMM 4.60, VTOL 1.44) without the VXE-SB-23-014 updates
FWAP link faults in the XCOMM log, later traced to GCS mission simulation (VXEP-220)

evidence.quote: @Cameron Chapman measured 305uOhms. After cleaning went down to 253uOhms. Both are failing numbers.
There is obvious damage to the AS150 contact. Anti-spark resistance measured 5.6 ohms.
Pass value is less than 180uOhms in production, 235uOhms in field
VTOL Log data shows a simultaneous voltage and current dropout
voltage dropped to as low as 7.5V.

team_root_cause:
Damage to Center Wing power connector (due to intermittent contact and/or sparking) resulted in battery voltage not reaching lift system. Backed up by VTOL log indicating a lift power failure (shows as low voltage).
https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VA-573

would_settle_it.what: Section or plating check of the 488 center wing AS150 contact to confirm poor plating (VA-573) versus incomplete mate as the initiating cause

reasoning: The VTOL log shows a simultaneous HLB voltage and current dropout to 7.5 V at the moment the lift system failed. The center wing AS150 contact was visibly damaged and measured 305 uOhm (253 after cleaning), above the 235 uOhm field limit. The corrective action ties it to the discrepant AS150 contacts contained in the factory, so poor contact quality is the most likely initiator, though an incomplete mate cannot be ruled out.
notes: Two aircraft involved: 487 fuselage with 488 wing set. The description says 90 ft, the report says the dropout was at about 110 ft AGL; the description says the forward two motors stopped before the aft two, which the report does not discuss. RMA induction PDF had no text.

event: VXE-380 (FBI training) climbed to launch altitude, then auto-aborted the launch and descended about 30 s after liftoff; the RPIC landed it safely.
component: GPS signal quality (SNR below RTL threshold)
failure_mode: GPS SNR dropped to 36 during the climb, below the RTL threshold of 40, so the VTOL AP triggered an automatic RTL as designed
contributing: LRF outage above about 120 ft (normal)
abort reason not shown to the operator

evidence.quote: GPS Status Byte (0x2E) indicates bad SNR. SNR at RTL is 36. RTL threshold is 40, so this caused the RTL
Once the GPS SNR value dropped below 40 the AC initiated automatic RTL and began descending.
this is a normal abort due to GPS loss prior to transition. Likely jamming or interference
he confirmed that it was the GPS that caused the RTL.

team_root_cause: Loss of GPS signal near transition altitude, system aborted launch per standard.

would_settle_it.what: Per-satellite CN0 and satellite count versus altitude, to tell local jamming or interference from an aircraft GPS antenna or receiver problem

reasoning: The log shows the GPS status byte flagging bad SNR, with SNR 36 against an RTL threshold of 40 at the moment of the RTL, so the abort worked as designed on a degraded GPS input. Why the SNR dropped is not shown; the team suspects jamming or interference since GPS was fine on the ground. The aircraft relaunched normally after an HLB swap.
notes: Designed abort, scored on the degraded GPS input. The pilot abort command came after the aircraft was already in its auto abort and had no effect. The ENG-3071 copy of the report is identical to the ticket attachment.

If vehicle condition will support it, we can try to reproduce the issue with the motor test panel similar to https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VXEP-426, it is possible the causes are related.  @Rajesh Budhabhatti @David Grosher @Cameron Chapman

That puts the start of the failure in the lift startup path, but the team could not separate VTOL AP command logic from ESC firmware because the booms were never returned. event: VXE-401 (INL, heavy 51 lb with wingtip antennas) had its VTOL launch aborted at about 30 ft, then hovered without responding to nudges, drifted onto a shed and slid off, breaking the tail and props.
component: VTOL AP landing logic (MultiLand.c mclandTrigger) with FW AP CommandRecover allowing Land Immediately during a launch abort
failure_mode: Land Immediately sent during an active launch abort started a second RTL; because the landing state was already set, the code never switched back to position update mode, so the aircraft held attitude only and drifted; continuous pause commands from the held controller trigger kept it from descending
contributing: wing oscillation in crosswind prompted the abort (VXEP-154)
aircraft flown at 51 lb, out of spec
abort trigger on the controller became the pause button while held
out of date FWAP and VTOL firmware flagged at connect

evidence.quote: This sequence results in the autopilot getting stuck in an attitude update only mode.
I have re-created this issue three times on a HIL.
During the second RTL mclandTrigger() is again called, but this time the state is already landing causing the execution to return false on line 152.
[07:16:08.694] vt lch abort request from gcs
[07:16:31.777] vt lnd now during vtol active

team_root_cause:
The landing drift occurred due to a software bug. If a “Land Immediately!” command is issued from the GCS during an active launch abort state, the aircraft will become stuck in an attitude update only mode. In this mode the aircraft will not update the horizontal position to maintain desired position.
The vehicle did not descend, during the aborted launch, due to receiving continuous pause commands sent to the aircraft from the GCS.
reasoning: The GCS debug log shows the launch abort at 07:16:08 and a Land Immediately during the active abort at 07:16:31, followed by over a hundred pause commands. Code review showed mclandTrigger returning early on the second RTL so position update mode was never restored, and the drift was recreated three times on a HIL and fixed with a patch. The failure to descend was due to the held pause commands.
notes: Both debug logs are under 300 KB; the crash log was read in full up to launch and the rest scanned with repeated status lines (landing override display, CMD PAUSE, RTL, version pings) filtered out. The 17 Oct log is a normal flight. The customer says the 16 Oct flight likely had the same behavior. The wing wobble on the same flight is tracked in VXEP-154. The FS2-1099 report file is titled VXEP-148 but covers 401.

event: VXE-398 (INL) fuselage overheated its main battery connector and burnt the connector O-rings twice during long ground power-ups with payloads, with two different batteries.
component: fuselage main battery AS150 anti-spark contact (aft fuselage power harness 107-102189-1)
failure_mode: high resistance anti-spark contact (488 uOhm, anti-spark tip-to-base 9.8 to 21.1 ohm) with a melted silicone ring and reflowed solder, heating at the main battery connector under steady ground load
contributing: aux payload (Vidar) on the top payload port drawing continuous load for hours
arcing damage on a MAIN BATT pin of the fuselage payload harness
logs supplied may not cover the event dates

evidence.quote: Measuring the contact resistance of the AS150 anti-spark contact came up with a value of 488uOhms.
The Main Batt AS150 Anti-spark silicon ring does indeed look melted
The running theory is that the resistor inside the anti-spark pin failed which will cause higher than normal contact resistance
4A pull through the fuselage power harness for 1 hour did not build up any excess heat at the AS150 connector.
We replicated the issues out at INL and we swapped it to another birds aux port and no issues so we assumed it was an aircraft issue at that point.

team_view_in_comments: The damage to that connector and no others strongly suggests an issue in the fuse power harness.

would_settle_it.what: Teardown and resistance test of the removed aft fuselage power harness 107-102189-1 and its anti-spark AS150, results not recorded

would_settle_it.file: VXEP-149 VXE398 Connector Hot and O-rings burnt - Investigation PPT.pptx
would_settle_it.what: Any later findings on the harness and anti-spark resistor on SharePoint

reasoning: The heat damage was at the fuselage main battery AS150 connector, which measured 488 uOhm (about twice the center wing field limit) with a melted anti-spark ring, and the problem followed the aircraft, not the battery or payload. The logs show only about 3 A steady draw, and a 4 A one hour test did not reproduce the heating, so the high resistance may be a result rather than the cause. Evidence reaches the fuselage power harness and its anti-spark contact but not a confirmed mechanism.
notes: VXEP-156 is a canceled duplicate of this ticket with the same three CSV files. The CSV summaries hold only column names and row counts. Customer and EA resistance readings disagree (0.9 ohm versus 1.0 MOhm positive to negative). No Root Cause field.

event: VXE-401 (INL, heavy with wingtip antennas) showed wing flapping oscillation in VTOL hover during the same launch that led to the VXEP-146 loss of control.
component: VTOL AP control loop (no notch filter for the ~8.4 Hz wing structural mode)
failure_mode: roll rate feedback couples with a wing structural mode near 8.4 Hz in crosswind hover and drives left-right lift throttle oscillation; seen aliased at about 1.7 Hz in the 10 Hz logs
contributing: wingtip antennas (8.1 oz left, 12.7 oz right)
aircraft at 51 lb
crosswind during launch
stiffer newer wing assemblies and lift booms

evidence.quote: yes I put this on Dave’s plate because we found the resonance in teh control lop (see the linked task).
This data shows a resonance mode between 7.9 - 8.7 Hz across the dataset.
Here is some data on the frequency of the oscillation, it appears to be at 1.7Hz
The plane is taking off with a crosswind (it drifts towards the shed, indicating wind direction) which lines up with what typically produces wing oscillations.
it seems that our stiffer wings and control system are prone to approaching resonance when faced with a crosswind.

team_view_in_comments: yes I put this on Dave’s plate because we found the resonance in teh control lop (see the linked task).

would_settle_it.what: Flight test results with the notch filter on a wingtip antenna configuration showing the wobble removed
ENG-3162 burst data at 100 Hz to confirm the mode and its coupling with roll rate feedback

reasoning: The 401 log shows a roll rate oscillation near 1.7 Hz, which matches the aliased image of the 7.9 to 8.7 Hz wing mode found in 100 Hz burst data on other aircraft. Earlier component swap tests showed wobble depends on the wing and boom hardware combination but needs the VTOL control loop and a crosswind to appear, and Flight Systems tied it to resonance in the control loop and designed a notch filter. The fix was not shown verified on 401, so this stays narrowed.
notes: Split from VXEP-146 (same flight). Cameron asked whether the control loop resonance caused the oscillation or was a related finding; no clear answer is recorded. The team judged the wobble not a safety of flight issue. No Root Cause field; the Issue Status says Flight Systems is investigating control loop resonance.
